name: Mesh API live capture (api.mochimo.org)
rule: Every response_body is what the endpoint returned, verbatim, to exactly request_body. Nothing is edited. NOT REPRODUCIBLE byte for byte -- balances and heights move -- and therefore EXCLUDED FROM THE REGENERATION CONTROL: tools/superset-check.py names this file as present-but-not-regenerated, and a re-run of this script is a new capture whose diff is read, never a control that passes.

oracle.why: The middleware is a recon source (reference/mochimo-mesh, errata 29): a third-party Go server whose replies record what one deployment did at one block, not what the protocol requires. A Rust codec agreeing with these bodies proves the codec speaks to this server as it was captured; it proves nothing about whether the server is right. The two hash vectors are set beside group D's C-recorded values in the tests, which is corroboration of the recon source and is deliberately not counted as an oracle for anything in this crate. The submit endpoint is never exercised: gaps.

gaps.rule: This capture records what the middleware answers. Two different things were once listed here as one want: whether a transaction this crate built was ACCEPTED, and whether the corpus can show that THIS CRATE built it. The first is answerable by reading a sealed block and is answered. The second is not answerable by reading a chain at all -- see N-submit-authorship.

N-submit-authorship.wanted: a capture taken AT SUBMISSION TIME by the process that submits: the request body sent to /construction/submit, the reply that came back, and the signed wire image as it left the builder -- recorded then, because no endpoint returns any of the three afterwards -- together with the block that later carried it.
N-submit-authorship.blocker: A CHAIN CANNOT TELL YOU WHO BUILT A TRANSACTION, and that is not a defect in this middleware or in this capture. A public ledger records what was accepted, not who assembled it: /block's rendering of the transaction this crate submitted is byte-identical to what it would be had any other wallet built the same spend, and no endpoint anywhere returns the raw signed bytes that would tie it to a builder (/mempool/transaction answers `Transaction not found` once mined; there is no handler that echoes a submitted image). A later session looking for a cleverer endpoint should know there is not one. The evidence has to be recorded by the process that sends the bytes, at the moment it sends them, which needs an operator-driven run -- every command after `create` reads /dev/tty (errata 172) -- on an account with a spendable balance.

vectors.note: the current block, as the middleware caches it; the capture's start block. The capture's found-tag vectors were taken while this index held (pin block).
a funded tag: result.address is the full 40-byte ledger address (tag then current hash), result.amount the balance as a JSON number. The tag sent is the address prefix.
the same tag through the balance endpoint: balances[0].value is the same figure as a decimal STRING; the handler resolves the tag with the same QueryTagResolve and discards the address.
the 40-byte address the resolve returned, through the handler's other arm (QueryBalance on the full address); the same figure again.

the SEALED block that carried the transaction session L3 submitted (errata 178). A block at a fixed height is served identically for ever, so this vector is byte-reproducible where every tip-keyed vector beside it is not: a re-run that changes it is a finding, not a refresh.

the same transaction alone, through the endpoint that serves one. Its metadata carries block_to_live; its SOURCE_TRANSFER metadata carries the two address hashes and the two totals, as decimal STRINGS.

the SAME transaction rendered by a different computation. /block re-parses the wire bytes on every request; /search replays rows the indexer wrote once, when the block was first seen. They disagree in two ways and both are correct: the source operation is the NET debit here and the GROSS debit there, with the change as its own operation; and the metadata values are decimal strings there and JSON numbers here, because both endpoints put them in an untyped map[string]interface{} and the Go expression's type leaks into the JSON. Served only when the deployment set EnableIndexer, which is false by default; absence is recorded in indexer_served rather than treated as a failure.

a balance asked for at the block BEFORE the spend. The reply echoes the current tip and the current balance: AccountBalanceRequest carries no BlockIdentifier field, so the request's is never read. This vector's VALUE is tip-keyed and nothing asserts it; what is asserted is the property -- the echoed index is not the one asked for.
the one network identifier the middleware serves.
versions and the advertised error table (codes 1-8; the declared code 9 is never returned and is not advertised).

vectors.note: an unfunded tag: the error object, code ErrAccountNotFound, HTTP 200.
a tag of the wrong width: ErrInvalidAccountFormat.
a tag that is not a string: ErrInvalidRequest.
network_identifier compared exactly: ErrWrongNetwork.
the only method is tag_resolve: ErrInvalidRequest.
an unfunded tag: ErrAccountNotFound.
neither 42 nor 82 characters: ErrInvalidAccountFormat.

the suggested fee the middleware advertises (Globals.SuggestedFee, floor 500) and the source balance it would fold into a server-built transaction. Read for the record; the Rust client builds locally and consults neither.
the reference's minimal valid image (group D, D1v), parsed by the Go reader: the only non-C implementation in the corpus that reads the C's bytes. Operations carry 20-byte tags and decimal amounts.
sha256 over all but the last 32 bytes: TX_HASH_ID as the middleware computes it.

the image group D's Ds1-N1 hashed with the reference's own tx_hash, so the Go answer here can be set beside the C-recorded id_hash. Agreement is corroboration of a recon source, not an oracle: this file's oracle block is the claim.
a body one byte over the middleware's 30 KB cap: what the gate actually answers.
